title: A Look at Fearsome Wilderness
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EkKqSnrdG7U

Daniel (@dungeondive) opens with Manly Wade Wellman and Silver John, the Appalachian balladeer who fights regional horrors with a silver-strung guitar. He reads "The Stars Down There" from Who Fears the Devil? in full. Then he turns to the game Wellman might have made: Fearsome Wilderness, a 1–4 player co-op in which Paul Bunyan, Johnny Appleseed, Babe the Blue Ox and Calamity Jane must survive twelve weeks until winter.

It plays as tower defence crossed with Yahtzee. Each hero rolls six dice up to three times, chasing food, water, axes and fighting symbols while dodging skulls. They plant trees that grow overnight, chop them for logs, and hold back the fearsome critters of folklore, from the splinter cat and the hodag to the agropelter and the Jersey Devil, as they march out of the darkness at the world's edge. The hardback rulebook nods to Kingdom Death: Monster. Its standout feature is the nightmares: draw a critter and read a short choose-your-own-adventure dream, rolling each step to wake up. In his example you climb a hill that turns out to be your own face.

The disappointment is that nothing carries over. You build the outhouse, the chicken coop and the cabin only on paper. There's no settlement phase, no gear and no stronger heroes. It feels like Kingdom Death with only the showdown, half a game in a box, and he was bored by the third scenario. He'll watch for the publisher's planned RPG.

----

Fearsome Wilderness lost Daniel because nothing you build carries between scenarios. How much does a sense of progression matter to you in a campaign game?
